questions.stem: The Repo Rate is the rate at which:

options.option_text: RBI lends money to commercial banks (short-term)
Commercial banks lend to customers
RBI borrows from commercial banks
Banks charge each other overnight

questions.explanation: Repo Rate (Repurchase Agreement Rate): rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities. Increasing repo rate makes borrowing expensive → reduces inflation.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks
Rate at which RBI lends to banks
Rate at which banks lend to customers
Rate for inter-bank overnight borrowing

questions.explanation: Reverse Repo Rate: rate at which commercial banks park excess funds with RBI. Higher reverse repo → banks prefer to park with RBI → less money in market → reduced liquidity.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was established in:

options.option_text: 1988 (statutory in 1992)

questions.explanation: SEBI established in 1988 as a non-statutory body; given statutory powers via SEBI Act 1992. Regulates Indian capital markets, protects investors, and promotes market development.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The term 'Inflation targeting' in India means:

options.option_text: RBI is mandated to maintain CPI inflation at 4% ± 2% (band: 2-6%)
Government controls all prices
Inflation is allowed to float freely
RBI targets wholesale price inflation at 5%

questions.explanation: Flexible Inflation Targeting (2016): India's monetary policy framework mandates RBI to keep CPI inflation at 4% with a ±2% tolerance band. Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) decides repo rate.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) requires banks to lend a minimum of what percentage of their ANBC to priority sectors?

options.option_text: 40% (domestic banks)

questions.explanation: Priority Sector Lending: domestic commercial banks must lend ≥40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sectors: agriculture, MSMEs, education, housing, export credit, weaker sections.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), launched in 2014, aimed to:

options.option_text: Provide universal access to banking services — a bank account for every unbanked household
Provide pension to all citizens
Give free crop insurance to farmers
Create 10 crore jobs

questions.explanation: PMJDY launched 28 August 2014: zero-balance accounts, RuPay debit card, overdraft facility, insurance cover. Over 50 crore accounts opened, transforming financial inclusion.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Central bank buying government bonds/securities to inject money into the economy and stimulate growth
Raising interest rates to control inflation
Reducing government spending
Devaluing currency to boost exports

questions.explanation: QE: non-conventional monetary policy where central bank creates money to buy long-term assets (bonds), lowering long-term interest rates and increasing money supply. Used post-2008 financial crisis.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, was enacted to:

options.option_text: Resolve insolvency of companies and individuals in a time-bound manner (180 days + 90 day extension)
Nationalise insolvent banks
Provide loans to bankrupt companies
Set up a bad bank for NPAs

questions.explanation: IBC 2016: consolidated insolvency law. Resolution process: 180 days (extendable to 270). If no resolution, liquidation. NCLT adjudicates corporate insolvency.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: GST (Goods and Services Tax) replaced which of the following taxes?

options.option_text: Central Excise Duty, Service Tax, VAT, CST, and several other taxes
Only income tax
Customs duty on all imports
Corporate tax

questions.explanation: GST (effective 1 July 2017) subsumed: Central Excise, Service Tax, VAT, CST, Octroi, Entry Tax, and others. It is a destination-based, multi-stage tax. Rates: 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's external credit rating is assessed by international agencies like:

options.option_text: Moody's, S&P, and Fitch (the Big Three)
World Bank
IMF
ADB

questions.explanation: Credit ratings: Moody's, Standard & Poor's (S&P), and Fitch Ratings. India's sovereign rating affects cost of borrowing internationally. Currently: Baa3/BBB- (investment grade, lowest tier).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which instrument, introduced by RBI in April 2022, replaced the reverse repo rate as the operative floor of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor?

options.option_text: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), the emergency lending window
Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), an uncollateralised deposit window
Bank Rate, the long-term reference rate set by the RBI
Special Drawing Rights (SDR), an IMF reserve currency allocation

questions.explanation: RBI introduced the SDF in April 2022 as a new floor for the LAF corridor; unlike reverse repo, it is uncollateralised — banks park surplus funds with RBI without receiving government securities in return. MSF is the ceiling (banks borrow from RBI against securities), not the floor. SDR is an IMF instrument unrelated to LAF.

questions.stem: NABARD was established in 1982 primarily on the recommendations of which committee?

options.option_text: Narasimham Committee on financial sector reforms (1991)
Shivaraman Committee on agricultural credit and rural finance
Kelkar Committee on direct and indirect tax structure reforms
Rangarajan Committee on balance of payments and capital flows

questions.explanation: NABARD was set up on 12 July 1982 based on the recommendations of the B. Sivaraman Committee (1979–81) to provide credit and development support for agriculture and rural sectors. Narasimham Committee (1991) dealt with banking sector liberalisation, not NABARD's formation.

questions.stem: RBI replaced the Base Rate system for pricing bank loans with a new benchmark effective April 1, 2016. Which benchmark was introduced?

options.option_text: Benchmark Prime Lending Rate (BPLR), linked to deposit costs
Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) framework
Prime Lending Rate (PLR), a discretionary rate set by each bank
External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) linked directly to repo

questions.explanation: MCLR, introduced from 1 April 2016, is calculated on the marginal (incremental) cost of funds rather than average cost, making it more sensitive to monetary policy changes. BPLR predated the Base Rate (pre-2010); EBLR was introduced later in October 2019 for retail and MSME loans and is distinct from MCLR.

questions.stem: Scheduled commercial banks are required to maintain their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) in which of the following forms?

options.option_text: Cash reserves deposited exclusively with the Reserve Bank of India
Gold, cash in hand, or RBI-approved unencumbered securities
Foreign exchange reserves and approved government bonds combined
Fixed deposits with public sector banks and Treasury Bills only

questions.explanation: SLR must be maintained in the form of gold, cash, or unencumbered approved securities (mainly government securities). Cash kept with RBI is covered by CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio), not SLR — a common confusion. Foreign exchange reserves are maintained by RBI itself, not by individual commercial banks as SLR.

questions.stem: Which banking model proposes that banks should invest depositors' funds ONLY in safe, liquid government securities and completely abstain from extending commercial loans?

options.option_text: Universal Banking, merging commercial and investment bank functions
Narrow Banking, restricting assets strictly to safe liquid securities
Shadow Banking, conducted by non-bank financial intermediaries
Islamic Banking, based on profit-sharing in lieu of interest payments

questions.explanation: Narrow Banking was proposed as a reform after the 1990s banking crisis in India; banks would hold only liquid government paper, eliminating credit risk but also curtailing credit creation. Universal Banking (full-service model), Shadow Banking (unregulated intermediation), and Islamic Banking (Shariah-compliant finance) are conceptually distinct.

questions.stem: Under Basel III norms adopted by RBI, banks must maintain a Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) above the minimum Common Equity Tier-1 (CET1) requirement to restrict payouts during stress periods. What is this mandated CCB as a percentage of Risk-Weighted Assets?

options.option_text: 1.5% of RWA, maintained entirely in Additional Tier-1 instruments
2.5% of RWA, held exclusively in Common Equity Tier-1 capital
3.0% of RWA, split equally between Tier-1 and Tier-2 capital forms
0.625% of RWA, representing one annual step in the phase-in schedule

questions.explanation: Basel III mandates a CCB of 2.5% of RWA, held in CET1 — the highest-quality capital. When a bank's CET1 falls into this buffer zone, dividend distributions and discretionary bonuses are restricted. Option D (0.625%) is the annual phase-in increment (2.5% ÷ 4 years), not the final requirement. Option C (3.0%) confuses CCB with the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), which is jurisdiction-specific.

questions.stem: The FRBM Act, 2003, amended in 2018 following the N. K. Singh Committee recommendations, permits the Central Government to invoke an 'escape clause' and exceed its fiscal deficit target on grounds such as national security or natural calamity. By how much can it deviate?

options.option_text: 0.25 percentage points above the prescribed fiscal deficit target
0.5 percentage points above the prescribed fiscal deficit target
1.0 percentage point above the prescribed fiscal deficit target
2.0 percentage points above the prescribed fiscal deficit target

questions.explanation: The N. K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended, and the 2018 FRBM amendment codified, that the escape clause allows a maximum deviation of 0.5 percentage points of GDP from the fiscal deficit target in a single year. The deviation must be placed before Parliament with reasons. 0.25% is the trigger threshold for Debt-to-GDP oversight under the same Act; 1.0% and 2.0% are not recognised thresholds.
